---
title: "Spectral analysis"
date: 2026-09-16
---

Spectral analysis was another self taught section, as it was not covered in the lectures. I worked through the spectral analysis tutorial we were given from start to finish, running the code and answering each question before opening the answer, and then added my own simulated example at the end.

**Period, frequency and aliasing.** The first idea is that a cycle can be described by its period $m$, the number of observations per cycle, or its frequency $f = 1/m$, the number of cycles per observation. A monthly annual cycle has $m = 12$ and $f = 0.0833$. The catch in R is that the `frequency` argument in `ts()` is actually the period, so monthly data is `ts(y, frequency = 12)`. The fastest cycle a series can show is $f = 1/2$, the Nyquist frequency, because you need at least two observations per cycle. Anything faster folds back into a slower frequency, so a true $f = 0.70$ looks exactly like $f = 0.30$ (period about 3.33). This is called aliasing and it cannot be fixed after the data has been collected.

**A series as a sum of waves.** This is the part I struggled with. I could not see how sine and cosine fitted into the periodogram. The idea is that any series can be written as a sum of waves at different frequencies, and each wave can be written as a cosine plus a sine, $a\cos(2\pi f t) + b\sin(2\pi f t)$. Writing it this way turns fitting a wave into a normal regression with two columns. It clicked when I tested it myself in Section 5. I regressed a simulated series on a sine and cosine pair at one frequency, and the size of the fitted pair matched the periodogram value at that frequency exactly (216.63 both ways). So the periodogram is the size of the fitted wave at each frequency, and it splits the variation of the series across frequencies like an ANOVA table with frequencies as the rows.

**Reading a periodogram.** The tutorial gives five steps. Convert the biggest peak to a period and give it in the units of the data. Check whether the other peaks are harmonics, because a repeating pattern that is not a pure sine wave needs peaks at $k/m$ to build its shape. A monthly December spike, for example, gives peaks at every $k/12$ even though it is one annual pattern. Do not trust a single tall value in the raw periodogram. In white noise the true spectrum is flat at 1, but single values reached 5.7 with $n = 1024$, and a bigger sample does not make them less noisy. So the next step is to smooth at a few spans and keep only what survives, and the last step is Fisher's test on the largest peak. For the period 24 series, 94% of the variation sat at one frequency ($g = 0.937$), so white noise was rejected.

**My own example.** For the last part of the tutorial I simulated eight weeks of hourly electricity demand. I built in a daily pattern with a morning and a bigger evening peak, lower weekends, a small trend and AR(1) noise. Before computing I expected the biggest peak at 24 hours. It was actually at 12 hours, because the morning and evening peaks are about 11 hours apart, so the daily shape looks a lot like a 12 hour wave. This was the harmonics step in practice: it is still one daily cycle with two peaks, not a separate 12 hour cycle. Every large peak was at $24/k$ or $168/k$ hours, so all the structure came from a daily and a weekly cycle.

**Takeaway:** spectral analysis holds the same information as the ACF, but it makes cycle lengths, and several cycles at once, much easier to see. It describes the cycles in a series but does not forecast, so it sits alongside ARIMA type models instead of replacing them. The main thing I will remember is to check for harmonics before reporting a peak as its own cycle.
